Recovery after a **periacetabular osteotomy (PAO)** is usually measured in **months, not weeks**.

A typical timeline is:

- **Hospital stay:** about **1–5 days** after surgery, depending on the center and your progress. ([yalemedicine.org](https://www.yalemedicine.org/conditions/periacetabular-osteotomy-pao?utm_source=openai))
- **Crutches / limited weight bearing:** often around **6–8 weeks**, sometimes longer if healing is slower or if you had additional procedures. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6090197/?utm_source=openai))
- **Basic daily function improves:** often by **2–3 months**.
- **Return to school/desk work:** commonly **4–8 weeks**, depending on pain, mobility, and commute demands.
- **Return to more normal activity / strengthening:** often **3–6 months**.
- **Full recovery:** commonly **6–12 months**, and some people keep improving up to about **1 year**. ([nm.org](https://www.nm.org/conditions-and-care-areas/treatments/ganz-osteotomy?utm_source=openai))

A few things can make recovery longer:
- having a **labral repair/hip arthroscopy** or femoral procedure at the same time,
- slower bone healing,
- needing more time to rebuild hip strength,
- pain sensitivity or nerve irritation,
- doing one hip vs. staged surgery on both hips.

A practical way to think about it:
- **First 2 weeks:** pain, swelling, getting around carefully
- **Weeks 6–8:** still protected, usually starting to advance weight bearing if X-rays look good
- **Around 3 months:** many people feel clearly better but not “normal”
- **Around 6–12 months:** closer to final result

Most people get back to everyday life about **3 months** after a periacetabular osteotomy (PAO). Feeling fully recovered usually takes **6 to 12 months**, and some people keep improving for up to two years.

**Typical timeline:**

- **In the hospital:** Usually 2 to 5 days, depending on the hospital. You will start physical therapy the day after surgery.
- **First week at home:** Plan on having someone to take care of you 24/7 for the first week.
- **Weeks 0–6:** Walk with crutches (partial weight bearing), and keep your wound clean. Many centers say you'll need crutches for 6 to 8 weeks.
- **Weeks 6–12:** Transition to one cane or crutch as instructed by your provider. You may start gentle stretching or strengthening exercises.
- **Around 3 months:** Most individuals return to school or work after three months.
- **After 6 months:** You may return to full activity (when the bone cuts are completely healed) except for running/jumping activities.
- **6–12 months:** Most people can resume athletics between 6 to 12 months. It usually takes 9–12 months to feel fully recovered.

answer.answerText:
Recovery from **rotator cuff surgery is usually measured in months, not weeks**. A common overall timeline is **about 4 to 6 months** for recovery, though larger tears, open surgery, or slower healing can make it take longer. ([medlineplus.gov](https://www.medlineplus.gov/ency/article/007207.htm?utm_source=openai))

Typical milestones are:

- **Sling/immobilizer:** often **4 to 6 weeks**. ([medlineplus.gov](https://www.medlineplus.gov/ency/article/007207.htm?utm_source=openai))
- **Physical therapy:** usually starts early, often in the **first week** or soon after, depending on the repair and surgeon’s protocol. ([hopkinsmedicine.org](https://www.hopkinsmedicine.org/health/conditions-and-diseases/rotator-cuff-tendinitis?utm_source=openai))
- **Basic daily activities:** often improve over **several weeks to a few months**, but with restrictions. ([medlineplus.gov](https://www.medlineplus.gov/ency/article/007207.htm?utm_source=openai))
- **Return to normal use / fuller recovery:** commonly **4 to 6 months**, sometimes longer for strength to fully return. ([medlineplus.gov](https://www.medlineplus.gov/ency/article/007207.htm?utm_source=openai))

What affects the timeline:
- **Size of the tear**
- **Type of surgery** (arthroscopic vs. open)
- **Tendon quality**
- **Your age and overall health**
- **How closely rehab instructions are followed** ([medlineplus.gov](https://www.medlineplus.gov/ency/article/007207.htm?utm_source=openai))

A simple rule of thumb:
- **Desk work:** sometimes **1–2 weeks**, if pain is controlled and the arm can stay protected
- **Driving:** only when your surgeon clears you
- **Manual labor / lifting / sports:** often **several months** ([medlineplus.gov](https://www.medlineplus.gov/ency/article/007207.htm?utm_source=openai))

answer.answerText:
Full recovery from rotator cuff surgery usually takes **4 to 6 months**. With a large or severe tear it can take up to a year. According to Hospital for Special Surgery, for small tears, full recovery time is about four months, for large tears, six months. For severe, massive tears, a complete recovery can take anywhere from 6 to 12 months.

**Typical timeline:**

- **Weeks 0–6 (protection):** Expect a sling with passive motion only for weeks 0-6, which means a therapist moves your arm for you. Some patients only need the sling for 2–6 weeks depending on tear size and tissue quality. Physical therapy often begins one week after surgery.
- **Weeks 6–12 (active motion):** You start moving the arm with your own muscles, building up gradually. Heavy loads are still off-limits. By 8-12 weeks post-surgery, most patients cross into what feels like "normal" recovery.
- **Months 3–5 (strengthening):** You add resistance bands and light weights. Patients can often return to most activities after about 12 weeks after surgery, but participation in vigorous sports may be restricted for four to six months.
- **Months 5–12 (full return):** This is when sports and heavy activity come back. For larger tears, full recovery may continue improving for close to a year.

**Returning to work and driving:**
- **Desk job:** You may be back within 1-2 weeks, but some sources say around 4 to 6 weeks after surgery.
- **Manual labor:** This can take anywhere from 3-4 months.
- **Driving:** Usually around 4–6 weeks. It can take longer if the surgery was on your dominant arm.

**Why it's so slow:** A rotator cuff repair reattaches tendon to bone, and that connection needs time to knit — generally several weeks before it can take any real load. If you push too early, the repair can fail.

**What affects your timeline:** Tear size, age, general health, job demands, and activity goals. Poor tendon quality can also make recovery longer. Lingering pain is normal. It is common to have shoulder pain, stiffness, and nighttime discomfort for several months after rotator cuff repair.

Your surgeon's rehab plan matters more than any general timeline, so follow it closely.
